claim: σS is a master transcription initiation factor that protects bacterial cells from various harmful environmental stresses including antibiotic pressure.
source: σS is a master transcription initiation factor that protects bacterial cells from various harmful environmental stresses including antibiotic pressure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about σS function.

claim: Full activation of σS-mediated transcription requires a σS-specific activator, Crl.
source: it is known that full activation of σS-mediated transcription requires a σS-specific activator, Crl.
evidence: This is stated as known information in the abstract.

claim: A 3.80 Å cryo-EM structure of an Escherichia coli transcription activation complex (E. coli Crl-TAC) comprising E. coli σS-RNA polymerase (σS-RNAP) holoenzyme, Crl, and a nucleic-acid scaffold was determined.
source: In this study, we determined a 3.80 Å cryo-EM structure of an Escherichia coli transcription activation complex (E. coli Crl-TAC) comprising E. coli σS-RNA polymerase (σS-RNAP) holoenzyme, Crl, and a nucleic-acid scaffold.
evidence: The structure determination is described in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: Crl interacts with domain 2 of σS (σS2) and the RNAP core enzyme.
source: The structure reveals that Crl interacts with domain 2 of σS (σS2) and the RNAP core enzyme, but does not contact promoter DNA.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: Crl does not contact promoter DNA.
source: The structure reveals that Crl interacts with domain 2 of σS (σS2) and the RNAP core enzyme, but does not contact promoter DNA.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis.

claim: Crl stabilizes key structural motifs within σS2 to promote the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: Results from subsequent hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) indicate that Crl stabilizes key structural motifs within σS2 to promote the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and also to facilitate formation of an RNA polymerase–promoter DNA open complex (RPo).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by HDX-MS experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: Crl facilitates formation of an RNA polymerase–promoter DNA open complex (RPo).
source: Results from subsequent hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) indicate that Crl stabilizes key structural motifs within σS2 to promote the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and also to facilitate formation of an RNA polymerase–promoter DNA open complex (RPo).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental approaches including stopped-flow fluorescence and KMnO4 footprinting.

claim: Crl activates transcription through a unique DNA contact-independent mechanism.
source: Our study demonstrates a unique DNA contact-independent mechanism of transcription activation, thereby defining a previously unrecognized mode of transcription activation in cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by structural and biochemical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: σS (also known as σ38 in Escherichia coli) is the master stress regulator that protects many Gram-negative bacteria from detrimental environmental conditions.
source: The alternative initiating σ factor, σS (also known as σ38 in Escherichia coli) is the master stress regulator that protects many Gram-negative bacteria from detrimental environmental conditions (Lange and Hengge-Aronis, 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: σS plays indispensable roles in the biofilm formation, virulence, antibiotic tolerance, and antibiotic persistence of human pathogens including Salmonella enterica, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and E. coli.
source: It also plays indispensable roles in the biofilm formation, virulence, antibiotic tolerance, and antibiotic persistence of human pathogens including Salmonella enterica, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and E. coli (Hansen et al., 2008; Murakami et al., 2005; Stewart et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Different stress conditions, including antibiotic treatment, could strongly induce the expression of σS.
source: Different stress conditions, including antibiotic treatment, could strongly induce the expression of σS (Battesti et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: σS-RNAP holoenzyme activates the transcription of ~10% of genes from the E. coli genome.
source: which in turn activates the transcription of ~10% of genes from the E. coli genome by the σS-RNAP holoenzyme, thereby rendering bacterial cells resistant to antibiotic treatment and other stresses such as hydrogen peroxide, high temperature, low pH, osmotic shock and so on (Battesti et al., 2011; Lelong et al., 2007; Weber et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: σS is a group-2 alternative σ factor.
source: σS is a group-2 alternative σ factor (Feklístov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: The conserved domains of σS (σS1.2, σS2, σS3.1, σS3.2, and σS4) interact with the RNAP core enzyme through exactly the same interfaces as those of housekeeping σ factor (σ70 in E. coli).
source: The conserved domains of σS (σS1.2, σ S2, σ S3.1, σ S3.2, and σS4) interact with the RNAP core enzyme through exactly the same interfaces as those of housekeeping σ factor (σ70 in E. coli) (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: σS shares a high degree of sequence similarity with σ70 and prefers similar sequences at the −10 (TATAAT) and −35 (TTGACA) promoter elements.
source: σS shares a high degree of sequence similarity with σ70 and prefers similar sequences at the −10 (TATAAT) and −35 (TTGACA) promoter elements (Gaal et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: The σS-RNAP holoenzyme tolerates degenerate promoter sequences (mostly at the −35 element) better than σ70-RNAP does, though at the cost of reduced overall transcription activity.
source: The σS-RNAP holoenzyme tolerates degenerate promoter sequences (mostly at the −35 element) better than σ70-RNAP does, though at the cost of reduced overall transcription activity (Gaal et al., 2001; Maciag et al., 2011; Typas et al., 2007b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: The amount of E. coli σS in cells is smaller than that of σ70 in stationary phase and stress conditions.
source: Besides the inferior transcriptional activity of σS-RNAP when compared to σ70-RNAP, the amount of E. coli σS in cells is also smaller than that of σ70 in stationary phase and stress conditions (Jishage et al., 1996)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: The affinity of σS is ~15 times lower than that of σ70 to the RNAP core enzyme.
source: and the affinity of σS is ~15 times lower than that of σ70 to the RNAP core enzyme (Maeda et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Crl was demonstrated to activate σS-mediate transcription directly both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Crl was demonstrated to activate σS-mediate transcription directly both in vitro and in vivo (Banta et al., 2013; Banta et al., 2014; Cavaliere et al., 2014; Cavaliere et al., 2015; England et al., 2008; Monteil et al., 2010a; Pratt and Silhavy, 1998; Typas et al., 2007a)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Crl-null Salmonella and E. coli cells displayed impaired biogenesis of curli, increased sensitivity to H2O2 stress, and reduced virulence due to decreased expression of several σS-regulated genes.
source: and Crl-null Salmonella and E. coli cells displayed impaired biogenesis of curli (which is important for host cell adhesion and invasion as well as for formation of biofilm), increased sensitivity to H2O2 stress, and reduced virulence due to decreased expression of several σS-regulated genes (Arnqvist et al., 1992; Barnhart and Chapman, 2006; Monteil et al., 2010a; Robbe-Saule et al., 2006; Robbe-Saule et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Crl shows highly stringent specificity to σS.
source: Crl shows highly stringent specificity to σS (Banta et al., 2013; Bougdour et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Crl broadly activates σS-mediated transcription in a promoter sequence-independent manner.
source: Crl broadly activates σS-mediated transcription in a promoter sequence-independent manner (Lelong et al., 2007; Robbe-Saule et al., 2006; Robbe-Saule et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Crl acts in at least two stages to boost σS-mediated transcription, namely the stage of σS-RNAP holoenzyme assembly and the stage of RPo formation.
source: and 3) Crl seems to act in at least two stages to boost σS-mediated transcription, namely the stage of σS-RNAP holoenzyme assembly and the stage of RPo formation (Banta et al., 2013; Bougdour et al., 2004; England et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Crl has been demonstrated to interact with σS2 and probably also with the RNAP core enzyme.
source: Crl has been demonstrated to interact with σS2 and probably also with the RNAP core enzyme (England et al., 2008)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: Crystal and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structures of Crl are available.
source: Although crystal and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structures of Crl are available (Banta et al., 2014; Cavaliere et al., 2014; Cavaliere et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citation support.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of E. coli Crl-TAC was determined at a nominal resolution of 3.80 Å by a single-particle reconstitution method.
source: The cryo-EM structure of E. coli Crl-TAC was determined at a nominal resolution of 3.80 Å by a single-particle reconstitution method (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The density map shows clear signals for the nucleic-acid scaffold, σS, and Crl.
source: The density map shows clear signals for the nucleic-acid scaffold, σS, and Crl (Figure 1B and D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 1.

claim: The crystal structure of Crl could be readily fit into the density, suggesting little conformational change of Crl upon interaction with σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: The crystal structure of Crl could be readily fit into the density, suggesting little conformational change of Crl upon interaction with σS-RNAP holoenzyme (Figure 1D) (Banta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Crl locates at the outer surface of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: The cryo-EM structure clearly shows that Crl locates at the outer surface of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Crl mainly interacts with σS2 and shields the σS2 through an interface of 695 Å2.
source: It mainly interacts with σS2 and shields the σS2 through an interface of 695 Å2
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: Crl contacts a helical domain of RNAP-β' clamp through a very small interface of ~85 Å2.
source: it also contacts a helical domain of RNAP-β' clamp through a very small interface of ~85 Å2 (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Crl approaches the upstream edge of transcription bubble, but makes no direct contact with the promoter DNA.
source: Crl approaches the upstream edge of transcription bubble, but makes no direct contact with the promoter DNA (Figures 1D–E and 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The mode of interaction between Crl and σS-RPo supports previous findings from genetic, bacterial two-hybrid, cross-linking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), NMR, or bioinformatic approaches.
source: Such a mode of interaction between Crl and σS-RPo supports previous findings from genetic, bacterial two-hybrid, cross-linking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), NMR, or bioinformatic approaches (Banta et al., 2013; Banta et al., 2014; Cavaliere et al., 2014; England et al., 2008; Monteil et al., 2010a; Monteil et al., 2010b; Pratt and Silhavy, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: A structural motif that includes helix α2 of σS1.2 (residues 72–82), σSNCR (residues 83–89), and helix α3 of σS2.1 (residues 90–93) is embedded into a shallow groove on Crl.
source: In the structure of E. coli Crl–TAC, a structural motif that includes helix α2 of σS1.2 (residues 72–82), σSNCR (residues 83–89), and helix α3 of σS2.1 (residues 90–93) is embedded into a shallow groove on Crl
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The 'specificity loop' of σS2.3 (residues 133–141) is anchored by Crl.
source: and the nearby 'specificity loop' of σS2.3 (residues 133–141) is further anchored by Crl (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Several Crl residues (P21, Y22, C37, L38, C41, F53, F76, and W82) create a hydrophobic patch in the shallow groove and make van der Waals interactions with residues (Y78, F79, R81, R82, L84, and R85) of σS.
source: Several Crl residues (P21, Y22, C37, L38, C41, F53, F76, and W82) create a hydrophobic patch in the shallow groove and make van der Waals interactions with residues (Y78, F79, R81, R82, L84, and R85) of σS (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Potential polar interactions between Crl (R24) and σS (D87) might contribute to the interaction.
source: Moreover, potential polar interactions between Crl (R24) and σS (D87) might also contribute to the interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: Most evolutionarily conserved residues of Crl are clustered in the shallow groove.
source: Intriguingly, most evolutionarily conserved residues of Crl are clustered in the shallow groove, implicating a functional relevance of its interaction with σS (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The Crl derivatives F53A and W82A rendered salmonella cells more sensitive to H2O2 stress.
source: Moreover, the Crl derivatives F53A and W82A rendered salmonella cells more sensitive to H2O2 stress (Monteil et al., 2010a), demonstrating the physiological importance of such an interface.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Mutating most interface residues (P21W, Y22A, R24A, L38A, F53A, or F76A of Crl; R81A, R82A or R85A of σS2) substantially impaired σS–Crl interactions.
source: The results show that mutating most interface residues (P21W, Y22A, R24A, L38A, F53A, or F76A of Crl; R81A, R82A or R85A of σS2) substantially impaired σS–Crl interactions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by yeast two-hybrid assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Alanine substitutions of R81, R82, or R85 of σS impeded its response to Crl.
source: Moreover, the results from an in vitro transcription assay show that alanine substitutions of R81, R82, or R85 of σS impeded its response to Crl
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Alanine substitutions of L38 or F53 of Crl impaired its ability to activate transcription.
source: and that alanine substitutions of L38 or F53 of Crl also impaired its ability to activate transcription (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A conserved 'DPE' motif within σS2 plays an indispensable role in its interaction with Crl.
source: Previous studies suggested that a conserved 'DPE' motif within σS2 plays an indispensable role in its interaction with Crl (Banta et al., 2013; Banta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: The 'DPE' motif is part of the 'specificity loop' of σS2, an essential structural element responsible for recognizing and stabilizing the unwound nucleotide at the most conserved position of promoter DNA (i.e. position −11 for σS and σ70-regulted promoters) in all bacterial transcription initiation complexes.
source: The 'DPE' motif is part of the 'specificity loop' of σS2, an essential structural element responsible for recognizing and stabilizing the unwound nucleotide at the most conserved position of promoter DNA (i.e. position −11 for σS and σ70-regulted promoters) in all bacterial transcription initiation complexes (Campagne et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: The 'specificity loop' encloses the NT-11A nucleotide.
source: In our structure, the 'specificity loop' encloses the NT-11A nucleotide as reported (Figures 2C and 4D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The side chain of Crl R51 reaches D135 and E137 of the conserved 'DPE' motif of σS2, and probably makes salt-bridge interactions with them.
source: The side chain of Crl R51 reaches D135 and E137 of the conserved 'DPE' motif of σS2, and probably makes salt-bridge interactions with them (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data, with speculation about the nature of the interaction.

claim: Mutating either D135/E137 of σS2 or R51 of Crl significantly compromised the Crl-σS2 interaction and Crl-mediated transcription activation.
source: Our results from yeast two-hybrid and in vitro transcription assays show that mutating either D135/E137 of σS2 or R51 of Crl significantly compromised the Crl-σS2 interaction and Crl-mediated transcription activation, highlighting the importance of such an interface (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Crl binds to two of the least conserved regions of bacterial σ factors: the σSNCR and the 'specificity loop'.
source: Our structure of Crl-TAC also explains the strict specificity of Crl to σS. Crl binds to two of the least conserved regions of bacterial σ factors: the σSNCR and the 'specificity loop' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Most Crl-interacting residues on σS are not present in σ70.
source: The sequence alignments of ten bacterial σS and ten primary σ factors clearly show that most Crl-interacting residues on σS are not present in σ70 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The density of Crl suggests possible interactions between Crl and the RNAP-β' clamp domain.
source: In agreement with the previous SPR results (England et al., 2008), the density of Crl also suggests possible interactions between Crl and the RNAP-β' clamp domain (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data and previous SPR results.

claim: The interface between Crl and RNAP-β' clamp is relatively small and only involves residues S10 and R11 of the Crl N-terminal loop.
source: The interface is relatively small and only involves residues S10 and R11 of the Crl N-terminal loop (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal loop of Crl shows only marginal effect on its activation of transcription.
source: Deletion of the N-terminal loop of Crl shows only marginal effect on its activation of transcription (left panel of Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Crl increases (~3.8 fold) the binding affinity between σS and the RNAP core enzyme.
source: We confirm that Crl is able to increase (~3.8 fold) the binding affinity between σS and the RNAP core enzyme in a fluorescence polarization assay using fluorescein-labeled σS (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An 'R loop'-mutated derivative of Crl completely lost its effect on the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: Moreover, an 'R loop'-mutated derivative of Crl completely lost its effect on the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme, whereas deleting the N-terminal tail of Crl moderately affects this assembly (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deleting the N-terminal tail of Crl moderately affects the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: Moreover, an 'R loop'-mutated derivative of Crl completely lost its effect on the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme, whereas deleting the N-terminal tail of Crl moderately affects this assembly (Figure 3B and Supplementary file 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Crl facilitates the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme mainly through its interaction with σS rather than through its interaction with the RNA-β' clamp.
source: Such results further suggest that Crl facilitates the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme mainly through its interaction with σS rather than through its interaction with the RNA-β' clamp.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: At the earliest time point (10 s), low deuterium incorporation (≤50%) was observed for most peptides from σS2 and σS4.
source: At the earliest time point, 10 s, low deuterium incorporation (≤50%) was observed for most peptides from σS2 and σS4 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The deuterium uptake of peptides from σS2 and σS4 increased gradually over time.
source: and the deuterium uptake of these peptides increased gradually over time (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: σS2 and σS4 generally adopt folded structures in solution.
source: Such facts indicate that these two domains generally adopt folded structures in solution, as observed in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS data.

claim: Most peptides from σ3.1 (except for those ranging residues 182–197) manifest high deuterium incorporation level (≥50%) at the earliest time point (10 s) and unchanged deuterium uptake up to 900 s.
source: Meanwhile, although σ3.1 appears to be folded in our cryo-EM structure (helix α6–α8), most peptides from these regions (except for those ranging residues 182–197) manifest high deuterium incorporation level (≥50%) at the earliest time point (10 s) and unchanged deuterium uptake up to 900 s (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: σ3.1 is largely solvent-exposed in solution.
source: indicating that σ3.1 is largely solvent-exposed in solution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS data.

claim: Helix α1 from σ1.2 (residues 56–67) and the σ3.2 linker (residues 218–245) generally appear to be solvent-exposed.
source: Consistent with their remote locations in the cryo-EM structure, helix α1 from σ1.2 (residues 56–67) and the σ3.2 linker (residues 218–245) generally appear to be solvent-exposed in the HDX-MS experiment (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The HDX profile of σS in the absence of Crl agrees well with a recent report.
source: The HDX profile of σS in the absence of Crl also agrees well with a recent report (Cavaliere et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Increased protection from HDX was consistently observed for peptides ranging residues 74–99 in the presence of Crl.
source: In the HDX-MS results, increased protection from HDX was consistently observed for peptides ranging residues 74–99 (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), which span helix α2 of σS1.2 (residues 74–82), σSNCR (residues 83–89), and the N-terminal part of helix α3 from σS2.1 (residues 90–99).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observed protection from HDX indicates that structural motifs from σS spanning residues 74–99 may locate at the interface between σS and Crl.
source: The observed protection from HDX indicates that these structural motifs from σS may locate at the interface between σS and Crl, which is highly consistent with our cryo-EM structure (Figures 1D and 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS data that is consistent with structural data.

claim: Increased protection from HDX was also observed for certain regions on α4 and α5.
source: Intriguingly, increased protection from HDX was also observed for certain regions on α4 and α5 (Figure 3D–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D), all of which locate away from the interface between σS and Crl as observed in the cryo-EM structure (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Crl imposes an allosteric stabilizing effect on σS.
source: Hence, besides directly shielding the motifs that span α2−α3, Crl seemingly also imposes an allosteric stabilizing effect on σS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS data showing protection in regions away from the direct interface.

claim: In the absence of Crl, typical bimodal shaped isotope clusters were observed for all peptides spanning 118–131aa and 148–161aa at longer time points.
source: To our surprise, in the absence of Crl, typical bimodal shaped isotope clusters were observed for all peptides spanning 118–131aa and 148–161aa at longer time points (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The maximum peak widths of peptides spanning 118–131aa and 148–161aa increased dramatically as the labeling period was prolonged, indicating an EX1 exchange mechanism in these regions.
source: Consistently, the maximum peak widths of these peptides also increased dramatically as the labeling period was prolonged (Figure 3F), indicating an EX1 exchange mechanism in these regions (Weis et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3F, with citation support for the interpretation.

claim: In the absence of Crl, regions on α4 and α5 underwent an unfolding event that is long enough to allow hydrogen-to-deuterium exchange to happen at all exposed residues.
source: Together, these sources of evidence suggest that, in the absence of Crl, the aforementioned regions on α4 and α5 underwent an unfolding event that is long enough to allow hydrogen-to-deuterium exchange to happen at all exposed residues (Wales and Engen, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS data, with citation support for the interpretation.

claim: Addition of Crl helps to restrain regions on α4 and α5 of σS2 in their low HDX conformation.
source: Addition of Crl apparently helps to restrain these regions on σS2 in their low HDX conformation (Figure 3E–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The HDX protection effect of Crl appears to be highly pronounced for peptides from α4.
source: and the HDX protection effect appears to be highly pronounced for peptides from α4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on HDX-MS data.

claim: α4 is one of the major anchor point on σS2 for the RNAP-β' subunit.
source: Notably, α4 is one of the major anchor point on σS2 for the RNAP-β' subunit (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The stabilizing effect rendered on helix α4 by Crl probably facilitates the docking of σS2 to the RNAP-β' subunit for subsequent proper positioning of other domains onto the RNAP core enzyme, thereby promoting the assembly of functional σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: Hence, the stabilizing effect rendered on helix α4 by Crl probably facilitates the docking of σS2 to the RNAP-β' subunit for subsequent proper positioning of other domains onto the RNAP core enzyme, thereby promoting the assembly of functional σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from HDX-MS and structural data.

claim: The increased rate of association during formation of σS-RNAP holoenzyme in the presence of Crl supports the hypothesis that Crl stabilizes σS2 to facilitate holoenzyme assembly.
source: Such a hypothesis is also supported by the increased rate of association that occurs during formation of σS-RNAP holoenzyme in the presence of Crl (England et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Crl is able to boost σS-mediated transcription at a step after σS-RNAP holoenzyme assembly.
source: A previous report suggested that Crl is also able to boost σS-mediated transcription at a step after σS-RNAP holoenzyme assembly (Bougdour et al., 2004; England et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation support.

claim: Crl increases the transcription activity of a pre-assembled σS-RNAP holoenzyme.
source: We here show that Crl increases the transcription activity of a pre-assembled σS-RNAP holoenzyme in an in vitro transcription assay (Figure 4A), supporting the previous finding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in vitro transcription assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The presence of Crl substantially increases the plateau fluorescence when σS-RNAP holoenzyme is mixed with promoter DNA in a stopped-flow fluorescence assay using Cy3-labeled promoter DNA.
source: The Cy3 fluorescence slowly reaches a plateau when σS-RNAP holoenzyme alone is mixed with promoter DNA; importantly, the presence of Crl substantially increases the plateau fluorescence (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Crl probably functions at the step of σS-RPo formation.
source: The results suggest that Crl probably also functions at the step of σS-RPo formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from stopped-flow fluorescence assay data.

claim: The presence of Crl greatly enhances the 2-AP fluorescence at plateau in a stopped-flow fluorescence assay using 2-AP-labeled promoter DNA.
source: The results in Figure 4C show that the 2-AP fluorescence increases slightly when pre-assembled σS-RNAP holoenzyme alone is rapidly mixed with promoter DNA; importantly, the presence of Crl greatly enhances the 2-AP fluorescence at plateau (Figure 4C), consistent with the above results using Cy3-fluoresence and confirming the effect of Crl on RPo formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The presence of Crl in the complex substantially increases the amount of RPo as measured by KMnO4 footprinting.
source: The results show a weak but site-specific cleavage in the expected T-stretch site when the σS-RNAP holoenzyme is present in the reaction (Figure 4D, lane 2); and again the presence of Crl in the complex substantially increases the amount of RPo (Figure 4D, lane 3), consistent with a previous report (Robbe-Saule et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by KMnO4 footprinting data shown in Figure 4D, with citation support.

claim: Crl uses its residue R51 to interact with D135 and E137 from the 'specificity loop' and secures the latter in a conformation that readily accepts the unwound nucleotide.
source: In our structure, Crl uses its residue R51 to interact with D135 and E137 from the 'specificity loop' and secures the latter in a conformation that readily accepts the unwound nucleotide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data, with citation support.

claim: Crl may facilitate RPo formation by pre-organizing or stabilizing a key helix-loop-helix element (α4-specificity loop-α5) of σS2.
source: Therefore, it is very likely that Crl may facilitate RPo formation by pre-organizing or stabilizing a key helix-loop-helix element (α4-specificity loop-α5) of σS2, and the 'specificity loop' in turn interacts with the first unwound nucleotide to facilitate promoter unwinding or to stabilize the transcription bubble during the subsequent steps of transcription initiation (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: Residue R129 from α4 may salt-bridge with the DNA phosphate backbone.
source: In the cryo-EM structure, residue R129 from α4 may salt-bridge with the DNA phosphate backbone (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on structural data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Residue Y145 from α5 sits just underneath the base of the unwound A-11, and might facilitate the flipping of A-11 by pi-stacking with its base.
source: Meanwhile, residue Y145 from α5 sits just underneath the base of the unwound A-11 (Figures 3G and 4F), and might facilitate the flipping of A-11 by pi-stacking with its base.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on structural data shown in Figures 3G and 4F.

claim: The rigidifying effect of Crl on helices α4 and α5 may promote not only the assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme but also the interaction between σS and DNA, which in turn contribute to promoter unwinding or RPo stability.
source: Together, such facts suggest that the rigidifying effect of Crl on helices α4 and α5 may promote not only the assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme but also the interaction between σS and DNA, which in turn contribute to promoter unwinding or RPo stability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: Crl functions as a stabilizing chaperon to facilitate the assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme and RPo formation.
source: Together, our biochemical data, cryo-EM structure and HDX-MS results clearly support a model in which Crl functions as a stabilizing chaperon to facilitate the assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme and RPo formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Crl shields a large and otherwise solvent-exposed surface on σS2 in the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and stabilizes the key 'specificity loop' of σS2.
source: The structure shows that Crl shields a large and otherwise solvent-exposed surface on σS2 in the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and stabilizes the key 'specificity loop' of σS2, but does not contact promoter DNA (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of structural findings.

claim: HDX-MS results recapitulate the interaction between Crl and the α2–α3 of σS2 in solution.
source: Subsequent HDX-MS results recapitulate the interaction between Crl and the α2–α3 of σS2 in solution, and further unravel that the stabilizing effect of Crl on σS2 extends beyond the helix α2–α3 to α4 and α5 (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of HDX-MS findings.

claim: The stabilizing effect of Crl on σS2 extends beyond the helix α2–α3 to α4 and α5.
source: Subsequent HDX-MS results recapitulate the interaction between Crl and the α2–α3 of σS2 in solution, and further unravel that the stabilizing effect of Crl on σS2 extends beyond the helix α2–α3 to α4 and α5 (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of HDX-MS findings.

claim: Binding of Crl stabilizes the conformation of σS to promote the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and the formation of RPo.
source: Considering the role of α4 and α5 of σS2 in anchoring the RNAP-β' subunit and promoter DNA, our cryo-EM structure and HDX-MS data thus point to a model in which binding of Crl stabilizes the conformation of σS to promote the assembly of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme and the formation of RPo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: Most bacterial transcription factors activate gene expression by creating additional physical linkage between RNAP and the corresponding promoter DNA.
source: Most bacterial transcription factors activate gene expression by creating additional physical linkage between RNAP and the corresponding promoter DNA (Browning and Busby, 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Eukaryotic transcription activators typically interact with both enhancer DNA element and mediator proteins, the latter bridging the transcription activators to transcription core machinery.
source: whereas the eukaryotic transcription activators typically interact with both enhancer DNA element and mediator proteins, the latter bridging the transcription activators to transcription core machinery (Jeronimo and Robert, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Crl activates transcription by stabilizing the critical structural elements of σS2: the 'RNAP-anchoring helix' and the 'specificity loop'.
source: Our structure and biochemical data reveal that Crl activates transcription by stabilizing the critical structural elements of σS2: the 'RNAP-anchoring helix' and the 'specificity loop'.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from structural and biochemical data.

claim: The effect of Crl on the 'specificity loop' is straightforward as Crl makes direct interactions with it.
source: The effect on the 'specificity loop' is straightforward as Crl makes direct interactions with it.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on structural data.

claim: Crl probably clamps the two helices (α2 and α3) of σS1.2 and σS2.1, reduces the internal motion of the helix bundle, and consequently stabilizes the conformer in a way that is competent for engagement to RNAP.
source: Although it is not known how exactly the signal of Crl binding is allosterically transmitted to the 'RNAP-anchoring helix', we infer that Crl probably clamps the two helices (α2 and α3) of σS1.2 and σS2.1, reduces the internal motion of the helix bundle, and consequently stabilizes the conformer in a way that is competent for engagement to RNAP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: Cartagena and coworkers recently reported a cryo-EM structure of a transcription activation complex comprising the E. coli RNAP core enzyme, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium Crl and σS.
source: We point out that Cartagena and coworkers recently also reported a cryo-EM structure of a transcription activation complex comprising the E. coli RNAP core enzyme, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium Crl and σS (Cartagena et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The structure of E. coli Crl–TAC agrees well with the chimeric complex structure reported by Cartagena et al.
source: Our structure of E. coli Crl–TAC agrees well with this chimeric complex structure, and both structures show that Crl engages σS-RNAP through a large interface with σS2 and a small interface with the RNAP core enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing the current structure with a previously reported structure.

claim: Cartagena et al. proposed a 'tethering' mechanism by which Crl tethers σS to the RNAP core enzyme and thus promotes σS-RNAP assembly.
source: Cartagena et al. (2019) proposed a 'tethering' mechanism by which Crl tethers σS to the RNAP core enzyme and thus promotes σS-RNAP assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: The interaction between Crl and the RNAP core enzyme only plays a partial role in σS-RNAP assembly.
source: By contrast, we found that the interaction between Crl and the RNAP core enzyme only plays a partial role in σS-RNAP assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on experimental data.

claim: Crl stabilizes critical structural elements of σS2 — the 'RNAP-anchoring helix' and 'specificity loop' — to promote σS-RNAP assembly and to facilitate RPo formation.
source: Instead, we demonstrate, using HDX-MS techniques, that Crl stabilizes critical structural elements of σS2 — the 'RNAP-anchoring helix' and 'specificity loop' — to promote σS-RNAP assembly and to facilitate RPo formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from HDX-MS data.

claim: Canonical bacterial transcription activators interact with the RNAP-α subunit and/or region 4 of σ factor.
source: Different from canonical bacterial transcription activators that interact with the RNAP-α subunit and/or region 4 of σ factor, Crl specifically activates the σS-regulated genes by making interactions with region 2 of σS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge about canonical bacterial transcription activators.

claim: C. crescentus GcrA, Mycobacterium tuberculosis RbpA, and Chlamydia trachomatis GrgA anchor RNAP through interactions with region 2 of primary σ factors.
source: A few recently discovered transcription activators, such as C. crescentus GcrA (Fioravanti et al., 2013; Haakonsen et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2018), Mycobacterium tuberculosis RbpA (Bortoluzzi et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2012; Hubin et al., 2017; Hubin et al., 2015), and Chlamydia trachomatis GrgA (Bao et al., 2012), also anchor RNAP through interactions with region 2 of primary σ factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Region 2 of σ factors could serve as a hub for docking various transcription activators.
source: suggesting that the region 2 of σ factors could also serve as a hub for docking various transcription activators.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from structural comparisons.

claim: GrgA and RbpA activate transcription by making essential interactions with promoter DNA in a sequence-independent manner.
source: However, in contrast to Crl, these transcription activators contain additional domains that activate transcription by making essential interactions with promoter DNA in a sequence-independent (GrgA and RbpA) or sequence-dependent manner (GcrA) (Bao et al., 2012; Fioravanti et al., 2013; Hubin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: GcrA activates transcription by making essential interactions with promoter DNA in a sequence-dependent manner.
source: However, in contrast to Crl, these transcription activators contain additional domains that activate transcription by making essential interactions with promoter DNA in a sequence-independent (GrgA and RbpA) or sequence-dependent manner (GcrA) (Bao et al., 2012; Fioravanti et al., 2013; Hubin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation support.

claim: Crl increases the transcriptional activity of σS-RNAP in a DNA contact-independent manner and through stabilizing the key structural elements of σS.
source: Collectively, we revealed here that Crl increases the transcriptional activity of σS-RNAP in a DNA contact-independent manner and through stabilizing the key structural elements of σS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: The combined effect of Crl — facilitating assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme and assisting RPo formation — would help σS to outcompete the housekeeping σ and substantially increase the transcription activity of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme in the expression of stress-related genes.
source: The combined effect of Crl — facilitating assembly of σS-RNAP holoenzyme and assisting RPo formation — would help σS to outcompete the housekeeping σ and substantially increase the transcription activity of the σS-RNAP holoenzyme in the expression of stress-related genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: The unique DNA contact-independent mechanism provides a new paradigm for bacterial transcription activation.
source: The unique DNA contact-independent mechanism also provides a new paradigm for bacterial transcription activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion about the broader significance of the findings.
